lead: Analog and mixed-signal blocks — amplifiers, filters, data converters, phase-locked loops — have no truth table and no clean stuck-at fault model. Their outputs are continuous, so a chip is judged by measuring specifications and comparing each result with a tolerance window. Digital test methods do not carry over: analog nodes are few, every measurement has noise, and test cost per pin is high. Hard faults are catastrophic; soft parametric faults pass a simple check but fail a specification. Structural tests such as IDDQ, oscillation and loopback give fast checks, while DNL, INL, SNR and ENOB describe converters. Every chip with an ADC, DAC or radio needs this test.
prereq: You need: test economics from 6.1; specification-based thinking from 6.8; converter circuits from an analog course.

sections.h3: Why digital test methods stop at the analog boundary

blocks.text: Digital circuits have finite values and a stuck-at fault model, so ATPG can target a specific fault (see 6.2 and 6.3). An analog node can sit at any voltage or current. Its correct value is a range: gain 10 ± 0.2, offset below 5 mV, output noise below 1 mV rms. Measurement noise and tester error eat part of that window. Few internal nodes are brought out because a probe adds capacitance and changes the circuit. Analog test cost per pin is high, and on a mixed-signal SoC it can dominate total test cost.

Faults are split into two classes. A hard fault is catastrophic: an open, a short, a stuck component. A soft fault or parametric fault is a drift: a resistor moves 20 %, a transistor loses gain, a capacitor leaks. The block may still pass a simple functional check but fail a specification. Soft faults are why analog test measures specifications, not just connectivity.

Structural tests give a quick check. IDDQ measures the quiescent supply current after the block settles; a short or bridge raises it. Oscillation test reconfigures the block as an oscillator; the frequency depends on component values, so a shift points to a fault. Loopback sends a digital pattern through a DAC, an analog path and an ADC, then compares the returned code with a tolerance (Figure).

Let an N-bit ADC have full-scale range FSR. One least significant bit is 1 LSB = FSR / 2^N. Offset error is the output at zero input, in LSB. Gain error is the slope error after offset is removed. DNL of code k is DNL_k = W_k / (1 LSB) − 1, where W_k is the measured width of code k. INL is the running sum INL_k = Σ DNL_i, the deviation from the ideal straight line. DNL = −1 LSB means W_k = 0: a missing code. SNR = signal power ÷ noise power, with harmonics excluded. SINAD = signal power ÷ (noise + distortion) power. Ideal SNR for a full-scale sine with ideal quantization = 6.02N + 1.76 dB. ENOB = (SINAD_measured − 1.76) / 6.02. Data sheets often label the SINAD column as SINAD or SNR+THD.

The servo ramp method slowly settles each code and records transition voltages; it is accurate but slow. The ramp histogram applies a linear ramp and counts hits per code; width is proportional to count, so DNL and INL come from counters. Sine-fit and FFT apply a pure sine, fit the ideal sine, subtract it, and transform the residue to the frequency domain; this gives SNR, THD and ENOB. Histogram and FFT methods are standard production tests.

sections.h3: Design for testability for analog blocks

blocks.text: Analog DFT adds access and control. Test points bring internal nodes to pins through unity-gain buffers, so the probe does not load the node. Bypass switches isolate a block: a filter can be switched out so the ADC is tested alone. Loopback is the mixed-signal workhorse: digital pattern → on-chip DAC → analog path (filter, amplifier) → on-chip ADC → compare with tolerance. It catches opens, shorts, gross gain loss and filter shifts. It cannot catch every fault: a DAC gain error and an ADC gain error of opposite sign can cancel in the digital code.

On-chip measurement puts a peak detector, RMS detector or small ADC near the block, so the external tester reads a digital number. This is analog BIST. IEEE 1149.4 is the analog companion of boundary scan: analog test cells at pins connect the pin to a two-line analog test bus, AT1/AT2, so an external instrument can force a voltage or current at the pin and measure the response. Only a few universities teach it; it helps board-level analog interconnect test.

figure.caption: Digital pattern → DAC → analog path → ADC → digital comparison. The returned code must lie inside a tolerance window, not match bit-for-bit.

spec.title: Loopback test of a mixed-signal block
spec.aria: Loopback path in which a digital pattern drives an on-chip DAC, the analog signal passes through the analog block and an ADC returns it to digital for comparison against tolerances.

examples.question: An 8-bit ADC has full-scale range 2.56 V. A ramp histogram gives measured code widths W64 = 14 mV and W65 = 6 mV. Take INL(63) = 0 LSB. (a) Find 1 LSB. (b) Find DNL at codes 64 and 65. (c) Find INL at codes 64 and 65. (d) A third code has measured width 0 mV; state its DNL and what it means.
steps: Number of codes = 2^8 = 256. 1 LSB = FSR / 2^N = 2.56 V / 256 = 0.010 V = 10 mV.

For measured width 0 mV: DNL = 0 mV / 10 mV − 1 = −1 LSB. The code never appears, so it is a missing code. INL at that code = INL(previous code) − 1 LSB. It is near zero only when INL before the code is about +1.0 LSB; otherwise the missing code shows up as a 1 LSB drop in the INL curve at that point.
examples.answer: 1 LSB = 10 mV; DNL(64) = +0.4 LSB, DNL(65) = −0.4 LSB; INL(64) = +0.4 LSB, INL(65) = 0.0 LSB; a 0 mV code has DNL = −1 LSB and is missing; INL at it is INL(previous) − 1 LSB.
examples.check:
FSR = 2.56
N = 8
codes = 2 ** N
lsb_v = FSR / codes
lsb_mv = lsb_v * 1000
w64 = 14.0
w65 = 6.0
dnl64 = w64 / lsb_mv - 1
dnl65 = w65 / lsb_mv - 1
inl63 = 0.0
inl64 = inl63 + dnl64
inl65 = inl64 + dnl65
dnl_missing = 0.0 / lsb_mv - 1
print(round(lsb_v, 2))
print(round(lsb_mv, 2))
print(round(dnl64, 2))
print(round(dnl65, 2))
print(round(inl64, 2))
print(round(inl65, 2))
print(round(dnl_missing, 2))

traps: DNL is not INL. DNL is the error of one code width; INL is the running sum of DNL. A large DNL can leave INL near zero if the next code has opposite DNL.

A missing code has DNL = −1 LSB, not INL = −1 LSB. INL at that code falls by 1 LSB from the previous code's INL. It looks near zero only if INL before it is about +1.0 LSB; check DNL from the histogram separately.
DNL and INL are defined after offset and gain errors are removed. A tilted transfer curve is gain error, not a large INL.
1 LSB is FSR / 2^N for an N-bit converter with 2^N codes; do not divide by 2^N − 1 unless the data sheet defines FSR that way.
SNR is measured with a near-full-scale sine, not with a DC input; a DC test says nothing about noise and distortion.

quiz.q: Define DNL and INL for an ADC.
quiz.a: DNL of code k is W_k / (1 LSB) − 1, the error of that code width against the ideal 1 LSB. INL is the running sum of DNL over codes, the deviation from the ideal straight line.

quiz.q: Why can a soft parametric fault pass a simple functional test?
quiz.a: A functional test checks that the block does something, such as producing an output for an input. A soft fault only shifts a value — gain, offset, delay or noise — so the output still appears but lies outside the specification window.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC has FSR = 4.096 V. A measured code has width 5 mV. Find 1 LSB and the DNL of that code.
A 12-bit ADC measures SINAD = 68.0 dB. Find its ENOB.
A code has DNL = −1 LSB but INL = 0.0 LSB at that code. Explain how this is possible.
quiz.a: The code is missing. If INL before it is +1.0 LSB, adding DNL = −1 LSB returns INL to 0.0 LSB. The running sum hides the missing code, so DNL from a histogram must be checked separately.

quiz.q: Why can a loopback test miss a gain error in the DAC or ADC?
quiz.a: Loopback compares the final digital code with the input pattern. If the DAC output is too high and the ADC also reads high by the same fraction, the two gain errors cancel in the digital code. The test then passes inside its tolerance even though each block is out of specification.

quiz.q: What does IEEE 1149.4 add to boundary scan?
quiz.a: It adds an analog test bus with two lines, AT1 and AT2, and analog test cells at pins. A cell connects the pin to the bus, so an external instrument can force a voltage or current at the pin and measure the analog response. This helps analog interconnect and some board-level analog tests.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production test of high-speed serial links uses on-chip loopback and eye-diagram measurement; RF blocks use modulated tests and spectral masks. Research is moving measurement into the chip with on-chip instruments and machine-learning calibration. Search for IEEE 1149.4, analog BIST, ADC histogram test and ENOB.
